Chapter 13 Vibration of continuous systems: string, shaft and beam

Chapter 13Lecture: Vibration of continuous systems: string, shaft and beam

1 Curvature is force: the wave equation of the string

We pull a guitar string aside with a finger and let go. It vibrates, and each of its points moves differently. What pushes each little piece of the string back? And how fast does a disturbance run along the string? Let us draw the answer to the first question, without a single formula.

First we draw three horizontal axes. Each is the string at rest, as we stretch it between two pegs. In our mind we cut a short piece out of the string and draw it above the first axis: straight but tilted, with an arrow \(T\) at each end. The arrows are the forces with which the neighbouring parts of the string pull it. We call this force the tension (sila napetosti) \(T\), because the string is stretched tight. They pull along the string, so they lie on one line and point apart. What is their sum? Two equal opposite forces on one line cancel, the resultant \(R\) is zero.

Now we bend the same piece into a hill. The pull at each end is again along the string, but the string tilts up at the left end \(a\) and down at the right end \(b\). So both arrows tilt down. The horizontal parts still cancel, the vertical parts add. What is left is a resultant downward, toward the axis.

On the third axis we draw a piece bent into a valley. The arrows tilt up and the resultant points up, again toward the axis.

This is the claim of this block in one sentence. A piece of string feels a force only where the string is bent, and the force is \(T\) times the change of slope across the piece. From this follows the wave equation (valovna enačba) \(\mu\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} = T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) (In the book: (13.2)), and shapes run along the string with the speed \(c = \sqrt{T/\mu}\) ((13.3)). This claim uses four things we have not explained. Why does only the bend count? Why is the force exactly \(T\) times the slope? How do we get an equation at every point from one piece? And why is \(\sqrt{T/\mu}\) a speed? We take them in turn.

1.1 Why does a straight string feel no force?

The straight piece may be far from the axis and steeply tilted. Why does nothing push it all the same? Everything rests on where the two arrows point. Why exactly along the string, along the tangent?

Take a slack thread and push it sideways with a finger. It does not resist, it only gives way. Now take it by both ends and pull them apart: only now does it resist, and it does so along itself. A thread can only pull, and only along itself. That is why the force at each end of the piece points along the tangent.

The thread is our first assumption: the string has no bending stiffness (upogibna togost). May we say that of a steel wire? The force that bending stiffness sets up when the wire is curved is of the order \(EI/L^2\), the tension is \(T\). For our string their ratio is \(8.3\cdot 10^{-6}\). The book calls this an order of magnitude estimate, not a calculation. When does it fail? When this ratio is not small: \(EI\) grows with the fourth power of the diameter, \(L^2\) and \(T\) are in the denominator, so for a thick, short or slack wire. The effect of the assumption: the force points along the tangent, and the term with \(EI\), which the beam equation has (13.6), drops out of the string equation.

Now back to the piece. On the straight piece the tangent at both ends is the same line. Then this is a tug of war in which both teams pull equally hard and the rope stays put: the resultant is zero, however steep the piece. On the hill the tangents at the ends are different lines, so the forces cannot cancel completely and a vertical resultant is left. So the force does not come from the displacement, nor from the slope, but from the difference between the directions at the two ends, that is from the bend.

1.2 Why is the vertical force \(T\) times the slope?

We know the direction of the force. But how large is it? Take the whole string and any piece of it.

We draw the axes and on the \(x\) axis the points \(0\) and \(L\), where the string is fixed. Our string, example A in the book, is a steel wire of diameter \(0.4\) mm and length \(L = 0.65\) m. Between them we draw the string at some time \(t\), with the slope greatly exaggerated so that we can see it. From it we choose a piece between the end \(a\) and the end \(b\), of length \(b - a\). The left neighbour pulls it with the force \(T\) along the tangent to the left, the right one with the force \(T\) along the tangent to the right. For our string \(T = 70\) N, and we draw the two arrows equally long. Up or down, though, the piece is accelerated only by the vertical components, so we draw them separately, in blue.

How large is a vertical component? The answer is a drawing of one triangle.

The slope (naklon) \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\) of the tangent says: when we go \(1\) to the right, we rise by \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\). That is simply what the word slope means. By Pythagoras the slanted side of this triangle is \(\sqrt{1 + w_{\mathrm{x}}^2}\) long, and it makes the angle \(\theta\) with the axis. Now we draw the pull \(T\) along the same tangent, at the same angle. We drop a perpendicular to the horizontal and get its vertical part. The triangles have the same angles, so they are similar: the vertical part is to \(T\) as \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\) is to \(\sqrt{1 + w_{\mathrm{x}}^2}\).

Here the second assumption enters, a small slope. For the string we take \(|w_{\mathrm{x}}| \le 0.01\), which is an angle of at most \(0.573^\circ\). At such a slope the hypotenuse is between \(1\) and \(1.00005\), so the vertical part equals \(T\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\) with a relative error of at most \(5\cdot 10^{-5}\). How much is that on the string? If the string has the shape of one sine arc, the middle is displaced by at most \(2.07\) mm. When does it fail? When we pull the string so far that the slope exceeds \(0.01\). What does the assumption do? Without it the force would be \(T\,w_{\mathrm{x}}/\sqrt{1 + w_{\mathrm{x}}^2}\), the equation would not be linear, and we could not simply add shapes.

The third assumption hides in both arrows \(T\) having the same length. Is that true? A bent string is longer than a straight one, so it stretches a little, and the tension grows a little. By how much? The hypotenuse is at most \(5\cdot 10^{-5}\) longer than the horizontal side, and that is the largest stretch. By Hooke's law the force grows by at most \(1.23\) N, which is \(1.8\) % of \(T\). The speed we are about to compute would at that force be larger by \(0.88\) %. That is the size of the neglected effect, not a bound on the error, and it holds for slopes up to \(0.01\). At a larger slope the effect is larger.

Now we have both ends: the vertical component at the right end is \(T\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(b)\), at the left end it is \(-T\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(a)\), because the left neighbour pulls to the left. Their sum is

\[F_{\text{vert}} = T\,\big(w_{\mathrm{x}}(b) - w_{\mathrm{x}}(a)\big) .\]

On the hill of the first picture this is exactly the difference of the two drawn slopes: \(w_{\mathrm{x}}(a)\) is positive, \(w_{\mathrm{x}}(b)\) negative, the difference is negative, the force points down. The horizontal resultant is not exactly zero, but at this slope it is at most \(1\) % of the same measure, and we neglect it, because the points of the string by assumption move only across. In the book: 13.1, steps 1 to 6, with a bound on the error in each step.

1.3 Why does one piece give an equation at every point?

Newton's law for the piece says: mass times acceleration equals the sum of the forces. The mass of the piece is the mass per unit length \(\mu\) times the length \(b - a\). For the string of example A, \(\mu = 9.802\cdot 10^{-4}\) kg/m, which comes from the density of steel and the cross-section of the wire. Since different points of the piece accelerate differently, we add mass times acceleration over the piece with an integral:

\[\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \mu\,w_{\mathrm{tt}}\,\mathrm{d}x = T\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(b) - T\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(a) .\]

On the left is mass times acceleration, on the right the two vertical components. In the book: (13.1).

We chose the piece freely. The right side can be written as a sum over the piece: the difference of the slopes at the ends is the sum of all the small changes of slope in between, that is the integral of \(w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) from \(a\) to \(b\). Both sides are now integrals over the same piece. The idea of the proof: if the difference \(\mu\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} - T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) were positive at some point, it would be positive on a very short piece around it too, and the integral over that piece would not be zero. Since the equation holds for every piece, even such a short one, the difference is zero everywhere:

\[\mu\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} = T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} .\]

In the book: 13.3.

Note that "every piece" is essential here. The book has an example of a motion for which the equation holds for the whole string but not for its quarter, because the leftovers of opposite signs cancel over the whole string. That is why we ask for the equation on every piece.

Two more assumptions sit in this step. The points move only across, so the piece is always the same matter over \([a, b]\) and the acceleration of a point is \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\). The string is homogeneous, \(\mu\) is the same everywhere, so we could write it as one number and in the end there is a single speed for the whole string. For these two the book gives no number. And the weight, which we did not draw? We show its number below, once we have the speed.

1.4 Why is \(\sqrt{T/\mu}\) a speed?

Only two numbers of the string appear in the equation, \(T\) and \(\mu\). What does their quotient measure? The unit gives the first hint. \(T/\mu\) has the unit \(\text{N}/(\text{kg/m}) = \text{m}^2/\text{s}^2\), so its root is in metres per second. We call it \(c\), the wave speed (hitrost valovanja). But the speed of what? Let us draw.

We draw the \(x\) axis, a long string. On it is a bump at time \(t\), the shape \(F(x - ct)\). After a time \(\tau\) there is the same bump, just as high and just as wide, only shifted by \(c\tau\) to the right. Why does it shift? The value of \(F\) depends only on \(x - ct\), and that stays the same if \(x\) grows by \(c\tau\) while \(t\) grows by \(\tau\).

Does such a shape satisfy our equation? We stand at one point and watch the bump ride past us. What we see in time is the shape in space, only driven past with the speed \(c\). Each derivative in time therefore brings one factor \(c\), two derivatives bring \(c^2\): \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} = c^2\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\). That is exactly the wave equation with \(c^2 = T/\mu\). In the book: 13.5.

Could a shape also move with some other speed? Suppose it shifts with the speed \(c' = 1.1\,c\). The shape would still keep its form, but it does not satisfy the equation: the acceleration would be \(1.21\) times too large for the force the curvature gives. That speed would hold only at a tension of \(1.21 \cdot 70 = 84.7\) N. The speed is not chosen by the shape, it is chosen by the string.

1.5 By numbers: our string

How fast is the wave on a real string, and what does the weight we left out cost? This view adds the sizes.

We draw the string between its ends, \(0.65\) m long. Near the left end we pull it into a bump and let go. How fast does it run? With the speed \(c = \sqrt{70/(9.802\cdot 10^{-4})} = 267.24\) m/s. To the right end it needs \(2.43\) ms, there and back \(2L/c = 4.86\) ms. If this repeats, it is one period with the frequency \(205.57\) Hz. This is not yet a proof, it is a forecast of the result of the next part.

Now the weight. Under the first string we draw the same string at rest and on it the weight, \(6.3\) mN for the whole string. That is \(9\cdot 10^{-5}\) of the tension. What does it do? Since the equation is linear, the weight only makes the string sag, in the middle by at most \(7.3\ \mu\)m, and does not change the motion about that sagged position. So the effect of the assumption is only a shift of the position about which the string vibrates.

1.6 What does it all stand on?

On which statements that need no further explanation does all this stand? If we follow every "why" to the bottom, we arrive at four.

  1. Mass times acceleration is the sum of the forces (Newton's second law), for a piece of string as for a stone.
  2. A thread can only pull, and only along itself (the pulled thread). Hence the arrows along the tangent.
  3. Two equal opposite forces on one line cancel, as in a tug of war. Hence the zero resultant.
  4. The vertical part of a slanted force is found by drawing a triangle similar to the slope triangle.

1.7 Back up

Can we now build the equation ourselves, from the ground up? Four lines on the board.

step what we get
vertical part of the pull at an end \(T\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\)
resultant on the piece \(T\,\big(w_{\mathrm{x}}(b) - w_{\mathrm{x}}(a)\big) \approx T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\,(b - a)\)
mass of the piece \(\mu\,(b - a)\)
the length \(b - a\) cancels \(\mu\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} = T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\)

The approximation in the second line is for a short piece, exactly the difference of the slopes is the integral of \(w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) over the piece, as we saw. Now back to the first picture. The hill has \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} < 0\) and is pushed down. The valley has \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} > 0\) and is pushed up. The straight piece has \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\) and nothing pushes it, even when it is tilted. So every bump is pulled back toward the axis. When it reaches the axis it has a velocity, so it overshoots and bends to the other side, where the force turns it again. That is vibration. The acceleration is proportional to the curvature (ukrivljenost), not to the displacement.

And the speed? A heavier string, larger \(\mu\), responds more slowly to the same force. A tighter one, larger \(T\), pulls back harder. Both together give \(c = \sqrt{T/\mu}\).

1.8 The view with two waves

What happens to a wave when it reaches a fixed end? This view adds what \(c\) means for a string with fixed ends. D'Alembert in 1747 gave the general solution of this equation as a sum of two shapes, one running left and one running right, and showed that with fixed ends only one arbitrary shape remains. Let us look at a plucked string.

We draw the axis, the string at rest, and the ends \(0\) and \(L\), a distance \(L\) apart. In the first row, \(ct = 0\), we pull the string at \(L/5\) into a triangle and let go. We split this triangle into two halves of equal height. One runs right, the other left, both with the speed \(c\). Their sum is the string. In the second, third and fourth row the waves have travelled \(0.1\,L\), \(0.2\,L\) and \(0.4\,L\). What happens at an end? The part of the shape that reaches past the end is turned upside down, so that the sum at the end is always zero. That is why the shapes are not chosen freely, which is d'Alembert's single arbitrary function. In the book: 13.2.

1.9 What we assumed

Which of these would give way first? Each assumption entered at its own place and has its measure there: no bending stiffness, a small slope, constant tension, no weight, motion only across and a homogeneous string. The largest of these measures belongs to the constant tension, \(1.8\) % of the force at the slope \(0.01\). In the book: 13.1, idealizations 1 to 6 and 13.2.

2 Modes: the shapes that fit between the ends

We pluck a guitar string. The string has infinitely many points, and each could swing in its own way. Yet we hear one clear tone with higher tones above it. Why exactly the frequencies \(f_1\), \(2f_1\), \(3f_1\)? We draw the answer on one picture, and this picture is also the explanation in one minute.

First we draw the two ends, short grey bars. The string is fixed there, so they do not move. The distance \(L\) between them is the length of the string, \(0.65\) m for ours. Now we draw a single arc, in blue. This is the string at its largest displacement. Half a period later the string is on the other side of the axis, grey dashed. What if we fit two arcs on the string? The point in the middle then stays at rest, it is a node (vozel). It also works with three arcs and two nodes. To the right of each shape we write its natural frequency: \(\omega_1\), \(2\omega_1\), \(3\omega_1\). A shorter arc is bent more and swings faster.

The claim in one sentence: between two fixed ends only a shape with a whole number of half-waves can swing in place, \(\sin(n\pi x/L)\) with \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = n\pi c/L\) ((13.6)), each swings like one mass on a spring, and every motion of the string is a sum of such shapes ((13.10)). This claim uses four things we have not shown. Why look for a shape that only breathes? Why a sine? Why whole numbers? Why a sum? We take them in turn.

2.1 Why look for a shape that only breathes?

What do we hear as a pure tone? A motion in which all points swing with the same frequency. Look at the first arc. If every point swings as \(\cos\omega t\), all points go up together and down together. The shape stays the same, only its size changes, from the blue arc to the dashed one on the other side and back. We write such a motion as \(w(x, t) = \varphi(x)\cos\omega t\): the shape \(\varphi\) times one single function of time. For systems with finitely many masses we called such a motion a mode (način nihanja, 8.140), here it is the same concept (13.6). So we look for a shape that only breathes.

2.2 Why a sine?

From the previous part we know what pushes a piece of string: the curvature. The force on a piece is \(T\) times the change of slope, per unit length \(T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\). What must the shape be like so that all points move together?

We draw the axis and on it the fixed ends. Between them we draw an arc of a sine, in blue. At one point we measure the displacement \(\varphi\) from the axis. Now we draw the force on the piece in the middle. The arc is bent most there, so the force \(T\varphi''\) is largest and points toward the axis. Closer to the ends the arc is bent less and the forces are shorter, each exactly as large as the displacement under it.

Why does this matter? If the force on every point is proportional to its displacement, every point is like a mass on a spring with the same stiffness per unit mass. They all have the same frequency and return to the axis together. So the condition is that the curvature is proportional to minus the displacement:

\[\varphi'' = -k^2\varphi , \qquad k = \frac{\omega}{c} .\]

This is equation (13.7). The sine is exactly the curve that is bent everywhere in proportion to its height. The book proves that there are no other solutions (13.7, steps 3 and 4): for the difference \(\psi\) of two solutions the "energy" \(\psi'^2 + k^2\psi^2\) is constant along the string and zero at the start, so the difference is zero everywhere.

Now a shape that does not work. Below the first axis we draw an axis with the same ends and on it a triangle, in orange. This is how a finger holds the string before we let go: we take it at \(L/5\) and pull it aside by \(1\) mm. The slope is at most \(0.0077\), below the bound \(0.01\) of the previous part. Where is the curvature here? Only at the kink. By the previous part the force is \(T\) times the change of slope, so here \(Ts\), where \(s\) is the jump of the slope at the kink. On the straight parts the force is zero, although they are displaced. So the kink accelerates toward the axis while the straight parts do not yet. The shape changes, the triangle is not a mode.

Where did we assume something here? The force is just \(T\varphi''\), because the string has no bending stiffness. We know the assumption and its measure from the previous part: the ratio of the forces is \(8.3\cdot10^{-6}\). Where that ratio is not small, the bending force of a beam adds to \(T\varphi''\) and the equation of the shape is no longer this one.

2.3 Why only whole numbers?

The equation \(\varphi'' = -k^2\varphi\) has the solution \(\sin kx\) for every \(k\), so at every frequency. What picks only some of them? The ends.

We draw one half-wave. It starts on the axis at the left end and comes back exactly to the axis at the right end. So do two half-waves, and three as well. Now we try one and a half half-waves, \(\sin(1.5\pi x/L)\), in orange. It solves the equation, since it is a sine. But at the distance \(L\) from the left end it does not come to the axis, it comes to \(-1\), so \(1\) mm below the axis for an amplitude of \(1\) mm. The end would have to move by that millimetre, but it is fixed. This shape does not work.

So the end \(x = L\) must be a zero of the sine. The zeros of the sine are at \(kx = \pi, 2\pi, 3\pi, \dots\), so \(kL = n\pi\) ((13.4), 13.7 step 5). A whole number of half-waves fits on the length \(L\), each \(L/n\) long. No theory is needed here, we only count: how many half-waves fit on the length so that none sticks out past the end.

The assumption: both ends are perfectly fixed. Why it holds: the model fixes the string rigidly at both ends ((13.4)), and the book gives no number for a real fixing. When it does not hold and what that does, we show at the end with a spring.

2.4 Why exactly \(f_{\mathrm{n}} = n\,c/(2L)\)?

We have the shapes. Where do the frequencies come from, and why are they exactly the multiples of the first? From \(kL = n\pi\) and \(k = \omega/c\) follows \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = n\pi c/L\), the frequency \(f_{\mathrm{n}} = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}/(2\pi) = nc/(2L)\). Let us see what this means on the third shape: a half-wave is three times shorter, so the arc is three times steeper and the curvature nine times larger for the same displacement. The force per unit displacement is nine times larger, and the frequency is its root, three times larger. The number of nodes is \(n - 1\), since \(n\) half-waves are separated by \(n - 1\) inner zeros.

For our string with \(c = 267.24\) m/s and \(L = 0.65\) m the first frequency is \(f_1 = 205.57\) Hz, then \(411.13\) Hz and \(616.70\) Hz (13.8). We tune the string with the tension. What happens if we tighten it by \(10\) %?

We draw the axes, the tension \(T\) across and the frequency \(f_1\) up. We mark the point at \(70\) N and \(205.57\) Hz, our string. Since \(c = \sqrt{T/\mu}\), the frequency grows with the root of the tension, the blue curve. At \(77\) N it is \(215.60\) Hz on that curve, only \(4.88\) % more. The proportionality that one of the book's sources states would be the orange line with \(226.12\) Hz, and it does not hold (13.2).

2.5 Why is every motion a sum of modes?

A plucked string is not a sine, it is a triangle. How does it swing then? The equation is linear: if two motions are solutions, so is their sum. So we build the triangle from sines, and each sine then swings with its own frequency.

Again we take the string at \(L/5\), pull it by \(1\) mm and let go. In the middle row we draw an axis with marks \(n = 1\) to \(8\) and over each \(n\) a bar, how much of mode \(n\) is in the triangle. The first is \(p_1 = 0.7444\) mm, the second \(0.3011\) mm, the third \(0.1338\) mm. The fifth is zero: at \(L/5\) the fifth mode has a node, and we took the string exactly there (13.14). The bars fall like \(1/n^2\), so the first three modes carry \(99.42\) % of the mean square displacement. That is why we hear one tone with a few higher ones.

We compute a coefficient by (13.8): we multiply the shape by the sine of the mode and integrate.

2.6 Why do the modes not disturb each other?

Why do multiplying and integrating give only the share of one mode and not a mix of all? Let us multiply two modes point by point and look at the area.

We draw an axis with its ends, on it the first mode in blue and the second mode in orange. The second has a node in the middle. Below we draw a new axis and on it the product of the two, point by point. Left of the middle both are positive, the product is above the axis, area \(+0.212\,L\). On the right the second is negative, the product below the axis, area \(-0.212\,L\). Why are they equal? Because the product is a mirror image: at the distance \(s\) left and right of the middle it has opposite values. The two areas cancel, the integral is zero.

This is so for every pair of different modes, not only these two: that is what the orthogonality theorem says ((13.72)). The idea of the proof: we integrate the shape equation by parts twice, and the term at the ends vanishes, since there the shape is zero or the force is zero. In the book: 13.7.2. So when we multiply the triangle by \(\sin(n\pi x/L)\) and integrate, all other modes give zero and only \(p_{\mathrm{n}}\) is left. Each mode is separate from the others and carries its own energy, like a separate mass on a spring.

2.7 The ground

Where did we stop? At statements that need no further explanation:

  • A fixed end does not move. That is what the word "fixed" means (the ends).
  • We count the half-waves that fit on a length (one, two, three).
  • A mass on a spring swings with one frequency (9), and a force proportional to the displacement makes every point such a mass.
  • Equal areas above and below the axis cancel (the product).

2.8 Back up

Can we now build the claim from the ground up? Force is curvature. For all points to move together, the force must be proportional to the displacement, and only a sine does that. The ends allow only whole numbers of half-waves, so the frequencies form a ladder \(n f_1\). The modes do not disturb each other, so from them, as from the rungs of a ladder, we build every plucked shape. Back to the first picture: the three blue arcs are the first three rungs, and there are as many nodes as the count \(n - 1\) predicts.

2.9 Two travelling waves

In the previous part we saw that a shape travels along the string with speed \(c\). How does that fit with shapes that stand in place? This view adds where the \(2L\) in the formula for the frequency comes from. There we split the plucked string into a wave running right and a wave running left, and their sum is the string. At an end a wave turns over and comes back. When each wave has run the path \(2L\), there and back, the shape is the same again as at the start. That takes \(2L/c = 4.86\) ms, and that is exactly the period \(1/f_1\) of the first mode. So a mode is a wave running back and forth between the ends, and the sum of the two directions stands in place ((13.11), 13.11). Hence \(f_1 = c/(2L)\).

2.10 Other bodies, the same three steps

Is this only the story of the string? No, the same three steps (the shape breathes, the equation of the shape, the ends pick the numbers) give the modes of the bar, the shaft and the beam.

In the left column is a bar fixed at both ends: a whole number of half-waves, as for the string. Now we let one end go, the middle column. A free end is not a zero of the shape, but there the shape has no slope, since at a free end there is no force. So not a whole number of half-waves fits on the length, but an odd number of quarter-waves. With two free ends whole halves fit again. The frequencies are \(c/(4L)\), \(3c/(4L)\), \(5c/(4L)\), the ratio \(1 : 3 : 5\) and not \(1 : 2 : 3\) (13.3).

The equation of a beam, however, is of fourth order, and its shapes are no longer plain sines (13.6). What does that do to the ladder? On a number line we mark the frequencies of the cantilever as ticks: the first two are at \(3.516\) and \(22.034\) times \(\omega_0\). The second is \(6.27\) times higher than the first, not twice. Below are the ticks of the beam clamped at both ends on the same line, the first only at \(22.373\). The ladder is there, but the rungs are not evenly spaced.

2.11 Assumptions and what they cost

Fixed ends (they enter at the whole numbers). What if an end is not fixed but sits on a spring?

We draw the axis, on the left the support, on the right the spring. The first mode and the second do not return to the axis at the right end, the spring stretches. So a whole number of half-waves does not fit on the length. From the numbers in the book (\(\lambda_1 = 4.1159\), \(\lambda_2 = 24.1393\), 13.7) the ratio of the frequencies is \(\sqrt{24.1393/4.1159} = 2.42\), not \(2\). The ladder \(n f_1\) is lost.

Small slope and constant tension (they enter at the sum). Why they hold: at a slope up to \(0.01\) the tension changes by at most \(1.8\) %, and our plucked shape has the slope \(0.0077\) (13.14). When they do not hold: when the slope exceeds \(0.01\). What that does: the equation is no longer linear and the shapes no longer add.

The sum fits the shape (it enters at the sum). For the triangle the coefficients fall fast, like \(1/n^2\). What about a shape that is not zero at the end, such as \(x/L\)? Its coefficients in the top row fall only like \(1/n\).

We draw the axes near the right end and the line \(x/L\) the sum should follow, and the end. The sum of five terms is smooth and falls toward zero. Twenty and a hundred terms fit the line better, but just before the end both jump to about \(1.18\). At the end every sum goes through zero, while the function is \(1\). The sines are all zero at the end, so they build well only shapes that respect the ends. The plucked string respects them, so its sum is exact.

3 A guessed shape gives the frequency from above

For a real part we almost never know the true shape of its vibration. What do we get if we simply guess it?

Take a steel bar and draw its axis \(x\). We clamp its left end, the right end stays free. It is one metre long. The bar vibrates along its axis, but we draw the displacement across it, so that we can see it. The shape of the lowest vibration is a quarter of a sine, we found that in the previous segment, and its frequency is \(1253.2\) Hz. Now suppose we do not know this shape. What does an engineer do? Guess. The simplest guess is the straight line \(v = x\). From it, by a formula we explain below, we compute the frequency \(1381.9\) Hz. That is \(1.1027\) times too high, so \(10.27\) %. The question of this segment: is it chance that we missed upwards? Why does a guessed shape never give a frequency below the true one, and how far above does it land?

The answer is one picture, a balance beam (tehtnica). It is also the few-minute explanation. We draw an axis on which we measure the ratio \(\lambda/\lambda_1\). Here \(\lambda = \omega^2\) is the square of the angular frequency and \(\lambda_1\) the square of the true lowest one. For this bar the true values lie at \(1\), \(9\), \(25\) and so on, since \(\lambda_{\mathrm{s}}/\lambda_1 = (2s - 1)^2\). The axis is broken after \(2\) and after \(9\) so that it fits on the board. Over the axis we lay the beam of the balance. At \(1\) we hang the weight \(w_1 = 0.98553\) on it. That is the share of our straight line that lies in the first mode. At \(9\) we hang the weight \(w_2 = 0.01217\), the share of the second mode, at \(25\) the weight \(w_3 = 0.00158\), and on and on infinitely many tiny weights. The weights are cubes of one metal, so a heavier cube is bigger.

Where does the balance balance? We must place the pivot at \(1.216\). This point is the quotient of our straight line divided by the true value, \(R(v)/\lambda_1 = 3/2.4674\). It is only \(0.216\) away from the first mode. The frequency is the square root of \(\lambda\), so the ratio of the frequencies is \(\sqrt{1.216} = 1.103\), exactly those \(10.27\) % too much. Left of \(1\) there is a wall: no weight hangs there.

The claim of the segment, on this picture: the Rayleigh quotient (Rayleighov količnik) \(R(v) = B(v, v)/\mathcal{M}(v, v)\) ((13.86)) of a guessed shape is the balance point of this balance. It is a weighted mean of the true \(\lambda_{\mathrm{s}}\), with weights that are not negative and add up to \(1\). So the pivot cannot move left of the wall, \(R(v) \ge \lambda_1\), and it reaches the wall only if all the weight hangs at \(1\), that is, if we guessed the true first mode. Under this claim are three questions. Why is the quotient a frequency squared at all? Why is it a weighted mean? Why can a mean not go below the smallest value?

3.1 Why is the quotient a frequency squared?

What does a quotient of two integrals have to do with a frequency? The answer is the energy, which during a vibration moves from stretch into motion and back.

Let the bar vibrate so that its shape stays the same and only swells and shrinks: \(w = v(x)\cos\omega t\). We draw the axis \(x\) and the clamp twice, for two moments. On the left is the moment \(t = 0\). The bar has the shape \(v\), the displacement is largest and the bar stops for an instant. The velocity is zero, all the energy is stored in the stretch. Its density is the square of the derivative \(v'^2\), the square of the strain, all of it together is \(\tfrac12 B(v, v)\). On the right is a quarter period later, \(\omega t = \pi/2\). The displacement is zero everywhere, so there is no stretch, but the velocity \(\omega v\) is largest. All the energy is kinetic, its density is \(\omega^2 v^2\), all of it together \(\tfrac12\omega^2\mathcal{M}(v, v)\).

Energy is conserved, so the blue area equals the orange one:

\[\tfrac12 B(v, v) = \tfrac12\omega^2\mathcal{M}(v, v) \quad\Rightarrow\quad \omega^2 = \frac{B(v, v)}{\mathcal{M}(v, v)} = R(v) .\]

That is why it is called a quotient: it divides one integral by another. The numerator is the stiffness of the shape, the denominator its mass, just as \(\omega^2 = k/m\) for a mass on a spring (9). This is the ground of this question: conservation of energy.

Assumption: no damping and small displacements. Why we may: without losses energy is conserved and the two areas really are equal, and small displacements give a linear model in which shapes add. When it fails: with damping part of the energy is lost during a period, the book does not estimate this effect with a number here. Effect: without it one area does not equal the other and the equation above is no longer exact.

Careful, with a guessed shape the bar does not vibrate like this at all. A bar released from the shape \(v = x\) does not vibrate in that same shape. The quotient is then only a number computed by the same formula. What this number tells us is the next question. In the book: 13.9.2.

3.2 Why is the quotient a weighted mean?

So the quotient of a guessed shape is only a number. What does this number measure? Let us take the guess apart into the true modes and see how much energy each brings.

From the previous segment we know that every shape is built from modes. Let us try it with the straight line. Again we draw the clamped bar over the axis \(x\) and on it the shape \(v = x\). The first mode alone is already close, the sum of the first three almost touches the straight line. So the straight line is \(v = \sum c_{\mathrm{s}}\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}\), where \(c_{\mathrm{s}}\) is the amount of the \(s\)-th mode in it.

Now the energy. Next to the vertical axis \(B\) we draw a column of height \(B(v, v) = 1\). We cut it into pieces. Each mode brings its own piece, \(\lambda_{\mathrm{s}} c_{\mathrm{s}}^2\): its own eigenvalue times the square of its amount. The first piece is almost the whole column, the first four together give \(0.9496\). The rest is a thin tail.

Why do the pieces simply add, with no mixed terms? Because the modes do not disturb each other. The product of two different modes has as much area above the axis as below it, that is the orthogonality of the previous segment ((13.72)). So all mixed terms are zero. The same holds for the mass, there each mode brings \(c_{\mathrm{s}}^2\). Let us write both on the board:

\[B(v, v) = \sum_{\mathrm{s}} \lambda_{\mathrm{s}} c_{\mathrm{s}}^2 , \qquad \mathcal{M}(v, v) = \sum_{\mathrm{s}} c_{\mathrm{s}}^2 , \qquad R(v) = \sum_{\mathrm{s}} \underbrace{\frac{c_{\mathrm{s}}^2}{\mathcal{M}(v, v)}}_{\mathrm{w}_\mathrm{s}}\,\lambda_{\mathrm{s}} .\]

So the quotient is the sum of the eigenvalues, each times its own weight \(w_{\mathrm{s}}\). These are the weights on the balance, and the pivot is their balance point. For the straight line \(w_{\mathrm{s}} = 6/k_{\mathrm{s}}^4\) with \(k_{\mathrm{s}} = (2s - 1)\pi/2\).

In general the proof gives only that the column is at least as tall as the sum of the pieces, the pieces never exceed it (point 1 of theorem 13.81). If the column holds more, the numerator is larger and the pivot moves even further right, away from the wall. This does not harm the bound. For the straight line the equality is exact.

Assumption: all the mass goes into the modes, \(\sum c_{\mathrm{s}}^2 = \mathcal{M}(v, v)\) ((13.87)), called completeness of the modes (polnost načinov). Why it is needed: without it part of the mass could lie in a shape that is not among the modes, and the sum of the weights would not be \(1\). When it holds: for the bar fixed at both ends or at one end and for the simply supported beam it is proved (lemma 13.80). For the cantilever and the beam clamped at both ends the book takes it from the source and does not prove it. Effect: there the bound is proved only under this assumption, the numbers confirm it, they do not prove it. In the book: 13.9.3.

3.3 Why can the mean not go below \(\lambda_1\)?

Why can an average not be smaller than the smallest of the numbers we average? Back to the balance. Each weight is a square, \(w_{\mathrm{s}} = c_{\mathrm{s}}^2/\mathcal{M}(v, v)\). A square is never negative, so no weight pulls the beam upwards. And all of them hang at \(1\) or to its right, since \(\lambda_1\) is the smallest eigenvalue. Where does a beam balance that has all its weights to the right of some point? Not there, it tips to the right. Every child on a seesaw knows this: if both sit on the same side of the pivot, the seesaw tips to that side. So the pivot is right of the wall, \(R(v) \ge \lambda_1\). This is the ground: a square is not negative and a mean of numbers is not smaller than the smallest of them.

When is the pivot exactly at the wall? When all the weight hangs at \(1\) and all other weights are zero, that is when the shape is the true first mode. An example follows at once.

3.4 Why is the guess so close?

A straight line does not look much like a quarter of a sine. Why is the frequency all the same only a tenth too high?

Look at the weights on the balance. The first is almost \(1\). The second is about eighty times smaller, the third almost eight times smaller again than the second, because the weights fall like \(6/k_{\mathrm{s}}^4\). Almost all the weight hangs on the first mode, so the pivot is only a little to its right.

The second thing is the square root. The quotient is \(21.6\) % above \(\lambda_1\), the frequency only \(10.27\) %, because the frequency is the square root of the quotient and the root roughly halves a small error.

And a better guess? This view adds how the pivot moves with the guess. Four boards.

On the first board is our bar with the straight line, under it the quotient \(3\,c^2/L^2\) and the true value \(2.4674\,c^2/L^2\). On the second board is a beam clamped on the left, a cantilever. As the guess we take its deflection under its own weight, which hardly differs from the true mode. The quotient is \(12.4615\) against the true \(12.3624\), only \(0.80\) % above, the frequency \(0.40\) %. On the third board is a simply supported beam. The guessed shape \(\sin(\pi x/L)\) is the true mode itself, so the quotient is exactly \(\omega_1^2\): the pivot is at the wall. On the fourth we again clamp a bar, take the shape and multiply it by a number. The quotient does not change, because the number cancels between the numerator and the denominator. Only the shape counts, not its size. The more the guess resembles the mode, the more weight hangs at \(1\).

3.5 Why must the guess hold the clamped end?

Does the balance hold for every line we draw? No. Let us see where it breaks down.

The balance holds only for admissible shapes (dopustno polje, 13.76): the shape is smooth enough and obeys the supports. Let us see what happens without this. On the first board we again draw the axis, the clamp and the straight line \(v = x\). Now we lift it, so that it is \(0.1\,L\) above the axis at the clamp. But the clamp says the bar does not move there. The slope is the same, so the numerator is the same. The denominator is larger, because we moved the whole bar and so added mass without energy. The quotient falls \(8.6\) % below \(\lambda_1\), the frequency is \(1198.2\) Hz, \(4.4\) % below the true one.

On the second board the same happens to the cantilever: to the deflection under its own weight we add a rotation, so that the shape has the slope \(0.1\) at the clamp, which the clamp does not allow. The quotient falls from \(12.4615\) to \(11.5766\), below the true \(12.3624\).

For the beam smoothness matters as well. On the third board we draw over the axis a shape with a kink. At the kink the slope jumps, and if we compute the second derivative piece by piece, we get a zero numerator and a zero quotient, which is nonsense.

Why does the bound break? When we take the shape apart into modes, a boundary term appears at the clamped end, which vanishes only if \(v = 0\) there. Without that the pieces of energy do not stay under the column, and the balance does not hold. In the book: 13.9.4. So admissibility is an assumption the bound needs: only then are the integrals really the energy and the mass of the body.

3.6 Why are finite elements above the true value?

In the earlier chapters the frequencies of finite element models with consistent mass were always too high. Was that chance?

On the first board we divide the bar into three elements, clamped on the left. Over each node we put a hat function, which is one at its node and zero at the others. Each of them is zero at the clamp. On the second board we add them with the values at the nodes and get the broken line \(u_{\mathrm{h}}\). A mesh is nothing but a guess built from hats. Since every hat is zero at the clamp, every such guess is admissible. For a beam we take node functions that are cubic piece by piece, with a smooth tangent at the node, so the guess has no kink and is admissible there too. The Ritz method picks among all broken lines the one with the smallest quotient, but it is still a guess. So the pivot stays right of the wall.

Let us check with numbers. We draw the frequency axis and on it the true value \(1253.2\) Hz, which is the wall. One element is our straight line, \(1381.9\) Hz. Two elements give \(1285.6\) Hz, four \(1261.3\) Hz, eight \(1255.2\) Hz. All dots are right of the wall and approach it. Left of it there is only the lifted line with \(1198.2\) Hz, which is not admissible.

And the higher frequencies, and the beam? We draw the error in percent against the number of the mode, on the left for the bar, on the right for the cantilever. Each row of points is one model: one element, two, four and eight. All points can be drawn on a logarithmic axis, which works only because all errors are positive. When we double the number of elements, the row moves down: for the bar the error falls about four times, for the beam about sixteen times.

Why can more elements not raise the estimate? A fine mesh contains all broken lines of the coarse mesh and more. The best guess in a larger set is at most better. That the bound holds also for the second, third and higher frequencies is stated by a theorem whose idea is the same balance on a shape orthogonal to the lower modes. In the book: 13.9.4 and 13.9.5.

Assumption: the mass is consistent and the integrals are exact. Why it is right: then the mass matrix really is the mass of the guessed shape, \(\mathcal{M}(u_{\mathrm{h}}, u_{\mathrm{h}})\), and the model is a true guess. When not: a lumped mass matrix is not the mass of any shape, and for a uniform bar fixed at one end with equal elements it gives a frequency below the true one. Reduced integration of the stiffness also spoils the bound. Effect: the bound from above is gone, the error can change sign.

3.7 Back to the top

Can we now answer the opening question ourselves? Let us build the answer from the ground up, on the balance. We guess an admissible shape. We take it apart into the true modes, each brings its own \(\lambda_{\mathrm{s}}\) and its own weight, which is a square and therefore not negative. Energy is conserved, so the quotient is a frequency squared, and since the modes do not disturb each other, it is exactly the balance point. The weights hang only at \(1\) and to the right, so the pivot is right of the wall. The weights fall fast, so it is close to it, only \(0.216\) away, and the root halves that error again. A finite element mesh is one of the guessed shapes, so it is above too.

One last limit of the claim. All this holds for the model with ideal supports. A real support is softer than the ideal one, so we expect the real frequencies to be somewhat lower than the computed ones (13.9.1). The balance says the estimate is above the frequency of the model, not above the frequency of the bar in the workshop.
